Sugar
Sugar is a class of <color=#3366CC>sweet-tasting</color>, soluble <color=#3366CC>carbohydrates</color>, many of which are used in food. Simple sugars, also called

<color=#3366CC>monosaccharides</color>, include <color=#3366CC>glucose</color>, <color=#3366CC>fructose</color> and <color=#3366CC>galactose</color>. Compound sugars, also called <color=#3366CC>disaccharides</color> or double
sugars, are molecules made of two bonded monosaccharides; common examples are <color=#3366CC>sucrose</color> (glucose + fructose),
<color=#3366CC>lactose</color> (glucose + galactose) and <color=#3366CC>maltose</color> (two molecules of glucose). <color=#3366CC>White sugar</color> is almost pure sucrose. During
digestion, compound sugars are <color=#3366CC>hydrolysed</color> into simple sugars.
Longer chains of saccharides are not regarded as sugars, and are called oligosaccharides or <color=#3366CC>polysaccharides</color>. <color=#3366CC>Starch</color>
is a glucose polymer found in plants – the most abundant source of energy in <color=#3366CC>human food</color>. Some other chemical
substances, such as <color=#3366CC>ethylene glycol</color>, <color=#3366CC>glycerol</color> and <color=#3366CC>sugar alcohols</color>, may have a sweet taste, but are not classified as
sugar.
Sugars are found in the <color=#3366CC>tissues</color> of most plants. <color=#3366CC>Honey</color> and fruits are abundant natural sources of simple sugars.
Sucrose is especially concentrated in <color=#3366CC>sugarcane</color> and <color=#3366CC>sugar beet</color>, making them efficient for commercial extraction to
make refined sugar. In 2016 the combined world production of those two crops was about two billion <color=#3366CC>tonnes</color>. Maltose
may be produced by malting grain. Lactose is the only sugar that cannot be extracted from plants, as it occurs only in
milk, including human breast milk, and in some <color=#3366CC>dairy products</color>. A cheap source of sugar is corn syrup, industrially
produced by converting corn starch into sugars, such as maltose, fructose and glucose.
Sucrose is used in prepared foods (e.g., cookies and cakes), is added to commercially available ultra-processed food
and beverages, and is used as a sweetener for foods (e.g., toast and cereal) and beverages (e.g., coffee and tea).
Globally, on average, a person consumes about 24 kg of sugar each year. North and South Americans consume up to
50 kg, and Africans consume under 20 kg.
The use of added sugar in food and beverage manufacturing is a concern for elevated <color=#3366CC>calorie intake</color>, which is
associated with an increased risk of several diseases, such as <color=#3366CC>obesity</color>, <color=#3366CC>diabetes</color> and <color=#3366CC>cardiovascular disorders</color>. In 2015
the <color=#3366CC>World Health Organization</color> recommended that adults and children should reduce their intake of free sugars to less
than 10% of their total energy intake, encouraging a reduction to below 5%.
Etymology
The <color=#3366CC>etymology</color> of sugar reflects the commodity's spread. From <color=#3366CC>Sanskrit</color> śarkarā, meaning "ground or candied sugar",
came <color=#3366CC>Persian</color> shakar and Arabic sukkar. The Arabic word was borrowed in <color=#3366CC>Medieval Latin</color> as succarum, whence came
the 12th-century <color=#3366CC>Old French</color> sucre and the English sugar. Sugar was introduced into Europe by the Arabs in <color=#3366CC>Sicily</color> and
Spain.
The English word jaggery, a coarse brown sugar made from <color=#3366CC>date palm</color> sap or sugarcane juice, has a similar
etymological origin: Portuguese jágara from the Malayalam cakkarā, which is from the Sanskrit śarkarā.
History
Sugar was first produced from sugar cane in the Indian subcontinent. Diverse species of sugar cane seem to have
originated from India (Saccharum barberi and S. edule) and New Guinea (S. officinarum). Sugarcane is described in
Chinese manuscripts dating to the 8th century BCE, which state that the use of sugarcane originated in India.
Nearchus (admiral of <color=#3366CC>Alexander the Great</color>), the Greek physician <color=#3366CC>Pedanius Dioscorides</color> and the Roman <color=#3366CC>Pliny the Elder</color>
also described sugar. In the mid-15th century, sugar was introduced into <color=#3366CC>Madeira</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Canary Islands</color>, where it was
mass-produced. <color=#3366CC>Christopher Columbus</color> introduced it to the <color=#3366CC>New World</color>, leading to sugar industries in Cuba and
Jamaica by the 1520s. The Portuguese took sugar cane to Brazil.
Beet sugar, the starting point for the modern sugar industry, was a German invention. Beet sugar was first produced
industrially in 1801 in Cunern, <color=#3366CC>Prussia</color>.
Sugar became a household item by the 19th century, and this evolution of taste and demand for sugar as an essential
food ingredient resulted in major economic and social changes. Demand drove, in part, the colonisation and
industrialisation of previously under-developed lands. It was also intimately associated with slavery. World consumption
increased more than 100 times from 1850 to 2000, led by the United Kingdom, where it increased from about 2 pounds
per head per year in 1650 to 90 pounds by the early 20th century.
Chemistry
Scientifically, sugar loosely refers to a number of compounds typically with the formula (CH2O)n. Some large classes of
sugars, ranked in increasing order of molecular weight are <color=#3366CC>monosaccharides</color>, <color=#3366CC>disaccharides</color>, or oligosaccharides.
Monosaccharides
Monosaccharides are also called "simple sugars", the most important being glucose. Most monosaccharides have a
formula that conforms to CnH2nOn with n between 3 and 7 (<color=#3366CC>deoxyribose</color> being an exception). <color=#3366CC>Glucose</color> has the
<color=#3366CC>molecular formula</color> C6H12O6. The names of typical sugars end with -ose, as in "glucose" and "<color=#3366CC>fructose</color>". Such labels
may also refer to any types of these compounds. Fructose, galactose and glucose are all simple sugars,
monosaccharides, with the general formula C6H12O6. They have five hydroxyl groups (OH) and a carbonyl group
(C=O) and are cyclic when dissolved in water. They each exist as several <color=#3366CC>isomers</color> with dextro- and laevo-rotatory forms
that cause polarised light to diverge to the right or the left.
• <color=#3366CC>Fructose</color>, or fruit sugar, occurs naturally in fruits, some root vegetables, cane sugar and honey and is the sweetest
of the sugars. It is one of the components of sucrose or table sugar. It is used as a <color=#3366CC>high-fructose syrup</color>, which is
manufactured from hydrolysed corn starch that has been processed to yield corn syrup, with enzymes then added
to convert part of the glucose into fructose.
• <color=#3366CC>Galactose</color> generally does not occur in the free state but is a constituent with glucose of the disaccharide lactose or
milk sugar. It is less sweet than glucose. It is a component of the antigens found on the surface of <color=#3366CC>red blood cells</color>
that determine <color=#3366CC>blood groups</color>.
• <color=#3366CC>Glucose</color> occurs naturally in fruits and plant juices and is the primary product of <color=#3366CC>photosynthesis</color>. <color=#3366CC>Starch</color> is converted
into glucose during digestion, and glucose is the form of sugar that is transported around the bodies of animals in
the bloodstream. Although in principle there are two <color=#3366CC>enantiomers</color> of glucose (mirror images one of the other),
naturally occurring glucose is D-glucose. This is also called dextrose, or grape sugar because drying grape juice
produces crystals of dextrose that can be <color=#3366CC>sieved</color> from the other components.
The <color=#3366CC>acyclic</color> monosaccharides (and disaccharides) contain either <color=#3366CC>aldehyde</color> groups or <color=#3366CC>ketone</color> groups. These
<color=#3366CC>carbon-oxygen</color> double bonds (C=O) are the reactive centres. All saccharides with more than one ring in their structure
result from two or more monosaccharides joined by glycosidic bonds with the resultant loss of a molecule of water
(H2O) per bond.
Disaccharides
Lactose, maltose and sucrose are disaccharides, also called "compound sugars". They share the formula C12H22O11.
They are formed by the condensation of two monosaccharide molecules with the expulsion of a molecule of water.
• <color=#3366CC>Lactose</color> is the naturally occurring sugar found in milk. A molecule of lactose is formed by the combination of a
molecule of galactose with a molecule of glucose. It is broken down when consumed into its constituent parts by
the enzyme lactase during digestion. Children have this enzyme, but some adults no longer form it and they are
unable to digest lactose.
• <color=#3366CC>Maltose</color> is formed during the germination of certain grains, the most notable being <color=#3366CC>barley</color>, which is converted into
malt, the source of the sugar's name. A molecule of maltose is formed by the combination of two molecules of
glucose. It is less sweet than glucose, fructose or sucrose. It is formed in the body during the digestion of starch by
the enzyme amylase and is itself broken down during digestion by the enzyme maltase.
• <color=#3366CC>Sucrose</color> is found in the stems of sugarcane and roots of sugar beet. It also occurs naturally alongside fructose and
glucose in other plants, in particular fruits and some roots such as carrots. The different proportions of sugars
found in these foods determines the range of sweetness experienced when eating them. A molecule of sucrose is
formed by the combination of a molecule of glucose with a molecule of fructose. After being eaten, sucrose is split
into its constituent parts during digestion by a number of enzymes known as sucrases.
Polysaccharides
Longer than disaccharides are oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. <color=#3366CC>Cellulose</color> and <color=#3366CC>chitin</color> are polymers, often
crystalline, found in diverse plants and insects, respectively. Cellulose cannot be digested directly by animals. Starch is
an amorphous polymer of glucose that is found in many plants and is widely used in the sugar industry.
Production
Due to rising demand, sugar production in general increased some 14% over the period 2009 to 2018. The largest
importers were China, <color=#3366CC>Indonesia</color>, and the United States.
Sugar
In 2022–23 world production of sugar was 186 million tonnes, and in 2023–2024 an estimated 194 million tonnes – a
surplus of 5 million tonnes, according to Ragus.
Sugarcane
Sugar cane accounted for around 21% of the global crop production over the 2000–2021 period. The Americas was the
leading region in the production of sugar cane (52% of the world total). Global production of <color=#3366CC>sugarcane</color> in 2022 was 1.9
billion tonnes, with Brazil producing 38% of the world total and India 23% (table).
Sugarcane is any of several species, or their hybrids, of giant grasses in the genus Saccharum in the family <color=#3366CC>Poaceae</color>.
They have been cultivated in tropical climates in the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia over centuries for the
sucrose found in their stems.
Sugar cane requires a frost-free climate with sufficient rainfall during the growing season to make full use of the plant's
substantial growth potential. The crop is harvested mechanically or by hand, chopped into lengths and conveyed
rapidly to the processing plant (commonly known as a sugar mill) where it is either milled and the juice extracted with
water or extracted by diffusion. The juice is clarified with <color=#3366CC>lime</color> and heated to destroy <color=#3366CC>enzymes</color>. The resulting thin syrup
is concentrated in a series of evaporators, after which further water is removed. The resulting supersaturated solution is
seeded with sugar crystals, facilitating crystal formation and drying. <color=#3366CC>Molasses</color> is a by-product of the process and the
fibre from the stems, known as bagasse, is burned to provide energy for the sugar extraction process. The crystals of
raw sugar have a sticky brown coating and either can be used as they are, can be bleached by <color=#3366CC>sulfur dioxide</color>, or can be
treated in a carbonatation process to produce a whiter product. About 2500 L of irrigation water is needed for every 1
kg of sugar produced.
Sugar beet
In 2022 global production of sugar beets was 260 million <color=#3366CC>tonnes</color>, led by Russia with 18.8% of the world total (table).
Sugar beet became a major source of sugar in the 19th century when methods for extracting the sugar became

available. It is a biennial plant, a <color=#3366CC>cultivated variety</color> of <color=#3366CC>Beta vulgaris</color> in the <color=#3366CC>family</color> <color=#3366CC>Amaranthaceae</color>, the tuberous root of
which contains a high proportion of sucrose. It is cultivated as a root crop in temperate regions with adequate rainfall
and requires a fertile soil. The crop is harvested mechanically in the autumn and the crown of leaves and excess soil
removed. The roots do not deteriorate rapidly and may be left in the field for some weeks before being transported to
the processing plant where the crop is washed and sliced, and the sugar extracted by diffusion. <color=#3366CC>Milk of lime</color> is added to
the raw juice with <color=#3366CC>calcium carbonate</color>. After water is evaporated by boiling the syrup under a vacuum, the syrup is
cooled and seeded with sugar crystals. The <color=#3366CC>white sugar</color> that crystallises can be separated in a centrifuge and dried,
requiring no further refining.
Refining
Refined sugar is made from raw sugar that has undergone a refining process to remove the molasses. Raw sugar is
sucrose which is extracted from sugarcane or sugar beet. While raw sugar can be consumed, the refining process
removes unwanted tastes and results in refined sugar or white sugar.
The sugar may be transported in bulk to the country where it will be used and the refining process often takes place
there. The first stage is known as affination and involves immersing the sugar crystals in a concentrated syrup that
softens and removes the sticky brown coating without dissolving them. The crystals are then separated from the liquor
and dissolved in water. The resulting syrup is treated either by a carbonatation or by a phosphatation process. Both
involve the precipitation of a fine solid in the syrup and when this is filtered out, many of the impurities are removed at
the same time. Removal of colour is achieved by using either a granular <color=#3366CC>activated carbon</color> or an ion-exchange resin.
The sugar syrup is concentrated by boiling and then cooled and seeded with sugar crystals, causing the sugar to
crystallise out. The liquor is spun off in a centrifuge and the white crystals are dried in hot air and ready to be packaged
or used. The surplus liquor is made into refiners' molasses.
The International Commission for Uniform Methods of Sugar Analysis sets standards for the measurement of the purity
of refined sugar, known as ICUMSA numbers; lower numbers indicate a higher level of purity in the refined sugar.
Refined sugar is widely used for industrial needs for higher quality. Refined sugar is purer (ICUMSA below 300) than
raw sugar (ICUMSA over 1,500). The level of purity associated with the colours of sugar, expressed by standard
number ICUMSA, the smaller ICUMSA numbers indicate the higher purity of sugar.
Forms and uses
Crystal size
• <color=#3366CC>Coarse-grain sugar</color>, also known as sanding sugar, composed of reflective crystals with grain size of about 1 to 3
mm, similar to kitchen salt. Used atop baked products and candies, it will not dissolve when subjected to heat and
moisture.
• Granulated sugar (about 0.6 mm crystals), also known as table sugar or regular sugar, is used at the table, to
sprinkle on foods and to sweeten hot drinks (coffee and tea), and in home baking to add sweetness and texture to
baked products (cookies and cakes) and desserts (pudding and ice cream). It is also used as a preservative to
prevent micro-organisms from growing and perishable food from spoiling, as in candied fruits, jams, and
<color=#3366CC>marmalades</color>.
• Milled sugars such as powdered sugar (icing sugar) are ground to a fine powder. They are used for dusting foods
and in baking and confectionery.
• Screened sugars such as <color=#3366CC>caster sugar</color> are crystalline products separated according to the size of the grains. They
are used for decorative table sugars, for blending in dry mixes and in baking and confectionery.
Densities
The densities of culinary sugars varies owing to differences in particle size and inclusion of moisture:
• Beet sugar 0.80 g/mL
• Dextrose sugar 0.62 g/mL ( = 620 kg/m^3)
• Granulated sugar 0.70 g/mL
• Powdered sugar 0.56 g/mL
Shapes
• Cube sugar (sometimes called sugar lumps) are white or brown granulated sugars lightly steamed and pressed
together in block shape. They are used to sweeten drinks.
• Sugarloaf was the usual <color=#3366CC>cone</color>-form in which refined sugar was produced and sold until the late 19th century.
Brown sugars
Brown sugars are granulated sugars, either containing residual molasses, or with the grains deliberately coated with
molasses to produce a light- or dark-coloured sugar such as muscovado and turbinado. They are used in baked goods,
confectionery, and toffees. Their darkness is due to the amount of molasses they contain. They may be classified
based on their darkness or country of origin.
Liquid sugars
• Glucose syrup and corn syrup are widely used in the manufacture of foodstuffs. They are manufactured from starch
by enzymatic hydrolysis. For example, corn syrup, which is produced commercially by breaking down maize starch,
is one common source of purified dextrose. Such <color=#3366CC>syrups</color> are use in producing beverages, hard candy, <color=#3366CC>ice cream</color>,
and <color=#3366CC>jams</color>.
• Inverted sugar syrup, commonly known as invert syrup or invert sugar, is a mixture of two simple sugars – glucose
and fructose – that is made by heating granulated sugar in water. It is used in breads, cakes and beverages for
adjusting sweetness, aiding moisture retention and avoiding crystallisation of sugars.
• Molasses and treacle are obtained by removing sugar from sugarcane or sugar beet juice, as a byproduct of sugar
production. They may be blended with the above-mentioned syrups to enhance sweetness and used in a range of
baked goods and confectionery including toffees and <color=#3366CC>licorice</color>.
• In <color=#3366CC>winemaking</color>, fruit sugars are converted into alcohol by a fermentation process. If the must formed by pressing
the fruit has a low sugar content, additional sugar may be added to raise the alcohol content of the wine in a
process called chaptalisation. In the production of sweet wines, fermentation may be halted before it has run its full
course, leaving behind some residual sugar that gives the wine its sweet taste.
Burnt sugars and caramels
Heating sugar to near 200 °C for several minutes yields a product called burnt sugar. Often additives are used to
modify the resulting caramels, e.g. <color=#3366CC>alkali</color> or <color=#3366CC>sulfites</color>. Several volatile products evolve in the heating process including
butanone, several furans (2-Acetylfuran, furanone, hydroxymethyl furfural), and levoglucosan and more.
Because sugars burn easily when exposed to flame, the handling of sugar powders risks dust explosion. The 2008
Georgia Imperial sugar refinery explosion, which killed 14 people and injured 36, and destroyed most of the refinery,
was caused by the ignition of sugar dust.
Other sweeteners
• Low-calorie sweeteners are often made of maltodextrin with added sweeteners. Maltodextrin is an easily digestible
synthetic <color=#3366CC>polysaccharide</color> consisting of short chains of three or more glucose molecules and is made by the partial
<color=#3366CC>hydrolysis</color> of starch. Strictly, maltodextrin is not classified as sugar as it contains more than two glucose molecules,
although its structure is similar to <color=#3366CC>maltose</color>, a molecule composed of two joined glucose molecules.
• <color=#3366CC>Polyols</color> are <color=#3366CC>sugar alcohols</color> and are used in chewing gums where a sweet flavour is required that lasts for a
prolonged time in the mouth.
Consumption
Worldwide sugar provides 10% of the daily calories (based on a 2000 kcal diet). In 1750 the average Briton got 72
calories a day from sugar. In 1913 this had risen to 395. In 2015, sugar still provided around 14% of the calories in
British diets. According to one source, per capita consumption of sugar in 2016 was highest in the United States,
followed by Germany and the Netherlands.
Nutrition and flavour
Brown and white granulated sugar are 97% to nearly 100% carbohydrates, respectively, with less than 2% water, and
no dietary fibre, protein or fat (table). Because brown sugar contains 5–10% molasses reintroduced during processing,
its value to some consumers is a richer flavour than white sugar.
Health effects
The World Health Organization and other clinical associations recommend that reducing the consumption of free sugar
(sugar sources added during manufacturing) to less than 10% of total energy needs can help to lower disease risk. This
amount of sugar consumption is equivalent to about 50 g or 12 <color=#3366CC>teaspoons</color> of added sugar per day. As of 2025, the
American Heart Association recommends that free sugar intake should be limited to 6% of total daily energy needs, or
36 g (9 teaspoons) for adult males, and 25 g (6 teaspoons) for women. In many countries, the source and amount of
added sugars can be viewed among ingredients on the labels of packaged foods. Added sugars provide no nutritional
benefit, but are a source of excess calories that can lead to overweight and increased disease risk.
Obesity and metabolic syndrome
A 2003 technical report by the World Health Organization provided evidence that high intake of sugary drinks (including
<color=#3366CC>fruit juice</color>) increases the risk of obesity by adding to overall energy intake. By itself, sugar is not a factor causing obesity
and metabolic syndrome, but rather its excessive consumption adds to caloric burden, which meta-analyses showed
could increase the risk of developing <color=#3366CC>type 2 diabetes</color> and metabolic syndrome in adults and children.
Cancer
Sugar consumption does not directly cause cancer. Cancer Council Australia have stated that "there is no evidence
that consuming sugar makes cancer cells grow faster or cause cancer". There is an indirect relationship between sugar
consumption and obesity-related cancers through increased risk of excess body weight.
The American Institute for Cancer Research and World Cancer Research Fund recommend that people should limit
sugar consumption.
Cognition
Despite some studies suggesting that sugar consumption causes hyperactivity, the quality of evidence is low and it is
generally accepted within the scientific community that the notion of children's "sugar rush" is a myth. A 2019
meta-analysis found that sugar consumption does not improve <color=#3366CC>mood</color>, but can lower alertness and increase fatigue
within an hour of consumption. One review of low-quality studies of children consuming high amounts of <color=#3366CC>energy drinks</color>
showed association with higher rates of unhealthy behaviours, including smoking and excessive alcohol use, and with
hyperactivity and <color=#3366CC>insomnia</color>, although such effects could not be specifically attributed to sugar over other components of
those drinks such as <color=#3366CC>caffeine</color>.
Tooth decay
The WHO, Action on Sugar and the Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition (SACN) state dental caries, also known
as tooth decay/cavities, "can be prevented by avoiding dietary free sugars".
A review of human studies showed that the incidence of caries is lower when sugar intake is less than 10% of total
energy consumed. Sugar-sweetened beverage consumption is associated with an increased risk of tooth decay.
Nutritional displacement
The "empty calories" argument states that a diet high in added (or 'free') sugars will reduce consumption of foods that
contain <color=#3366CC>essential nutrients</color>. This nutrient displacement occurs if sugar makes up more than 25% of daily energy intake,
a proportion associated with poor diet quality and risk of obesity. Displacement may occur at lower levels of
consumption.
Recommended dietary intake
The WHO recommends that both adults and children reduce the intake of free sugars to less than 10% of total energy
intake. "Free sugars" include monosaccharides and disaccharides added to foods, and sugars found in fruit juice and
concentrates, as well as in honey and syrups.
On 20 May 2016, the United States Food and Drug Administration announced changes to the Nutrition Facts panel
displayed on all foods, to be effective by July 2018. New to the panel is a requirement to list "added sugars" by weight
and as a percentage of Daily Value (DV). For vitamins and minerals, the intent of DVs is to indicate how much should
be consumed. For added sugars, the guidance is that 100% DV should not be exceeded. 100% DV is defined as 50
grams. For a person consuming 2000 calories a day, 50 grams is equal to 200 calories and thus 10% of total calories –
the same guidance as the WHO. To put this in context, most 12 USfloz cans of soda contain 39 grams of sugar. In the
United States, a government survey on food consumption in 2013–14 reported that, for men and women aged 20 and
older, the average total sugar intakes – naturally occurring in foods and added – were, respectively, 125 and 99 grams
per day. The American Heart Association recommends even lower daily consumption of added sugars: 36 grams for
men and 25 grams for women.
Society and culture
Manufacturers of sugary products, such as soft drinks and candy, and the Sugar Research Foundation have been
accused of trying to influence consumers and medical associations in the 1960s and 1970s by creating doubt about the
potential health hazards of sucrose overconsumption, while promoting saturated fat as the main dietary risk factor in
<color=#3366CC>cardiovascular diseases</color>. In 2016, the criticism led to recommendations that diet <color=#3366CC>policymakers</color> emphasise the need for
high-quality research that accounts for multiple biomarkers on development of cardiovascular diseases.
Originally, no sugar was white; the anthropologist <color=#3366CC>Sidney Mintz</color> writes that white likely became understood as the ideal
after groups who associated the colour white with purity transferred their value to sugar. In India, sugar frequently
appears in religious observances. For ritual purity, such sugar cannot be white.
In interstellar space
As sugar could not have been easily formed under the extreme environment of early Earth, it has been suggested that
certain sugars may have originated from space. <color=#3366CC>Astronomers</color> postulate that <color=#3366CC>asteroids</color> delivered sugars to Earth, or
sugars were always present in the <color=#3366CC>Solar System</color>.
In 2000, astronomers detected glycolaldehyde—a sugar-like molecule—in <color=#3366CC>interstellar space</color>. True sugar was first
collected from an asteroid in 2019. Sugar was also detected in a sample collected from the asteroid 101955 Bennu in
In 2026, erythrulose—a tetrose <color=#3366CC>monosaccharide</color>—was detected in dust grains of a <color=#3366CC>molecular cloud</color> near the center of
the <color=#3366CC>Milky Way</color>, marking the first time a sugar molecule was found in interstellar space. The identification of erythrulose
in <color=#3366CC>galactic</color> dust indicates its possible involvement in forming sugar-containing <color=#3366CC>nucleic acids</color> during the <color=#3366CC>origin of life on</color>
<color=#3366CC>Earth</color> about four billion years ago.
Western United States
The Western United States (also called the American West, the Western States, the Far West, the Western territories,
and the West) is one of the four census regions defined by the United States Census Bureau.
As American settlement in the U.S. <color=#3366CC>expanded westward</color>, the meaning of the term the West changed. Before around
1800, the crest of the <color=#3366CC>Appalachian Mountains</color> was seen as the <color=#3366CC>western frontier</color>. The frontier moved westward and
eventually the lands west of the <color=#3366CC>Mississippi River</color> were considered the West.
The U.S. Census Bureau's definition of the 13 westernmost states includes the <color=#3366CC>Rocky Mountains</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Great Basin</color>
to the Pacific Coast, Alaska and the mid-Pacific islands state, Hawaii. To the east of the Western United States is the
<color=#3366CC>Midwestern United States</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Southern United States</color>, with <color=#3366CC>Canada</color> to the north and <color=#3366CC>Mexico</color> to the south.

The West contains several major <color=#3366CC>biomes</color>, including arid and <color=#3366CC>semi-arid</color> <color=#3366CC>plateaus</color> and <color=#3366CC>plains</color>, particularly in the <color=#3366CC>American</color>

<color=#3366CC>Southwest</color>; <color=#3366CC>forested</color> <color=#3366CC>mountains</color>, including three major ranges, the <color=#3366CC>Sierra Nevada</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Cascades</color>, and Rocky Mountains;
the long <color=#3366CC>coastal shoreline</color> of the Pacific Coast; and the <color=#3366CC>rainforests</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Northwest</color>.
Geographic definition
The Western United States is the largest region of the country, covering nearly half the land area of the contiguous
<color=#3366CC>United States</color>. It is also the most geographically diverse, incorporating geographic regions such as the <color=#3366CC>temperate</color>

<color=#3366CC>rainforests</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Northwest</color>, the highest mountain ranges, including the <color=#3366CC>Rocky Mountains</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Sierra Nevada</color>, and the
<color=#3366CC>Cascade Range</color>, numerous glaciers, and the western edge of the <color=#3366CC>Great Plains</color>. It also contains the majority of the
desert areas located in the United States. The <color=#3366CC>Mojave</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Great Basin</color> deserts lie entirely within the Western
region, along with parts of the <color=#3366CC>Sonoran</color> and <color=#3366CC>Chihuahuan</color> deserts (the latter extends significantly into Texas, while both
extend into <color=#3366CC>Mexico</color>). Given this expansive and diverse geography it is no wonder that the region is difficult to define
precisely. Sensing a possible shift in the popular understanding of the West as a region in the early 1990s, historian
Walter Nugent conducted a survey of three groups of professionals with ties to the region: a large group of Western
historians (187 respondents), and two smaller groups, 25 journalists and publishers and 39 Western authors. A majority
of the historian respondents placed the eastern boundary of the West east of the Census definition out on the eastern
edge of the Great Plains or on the <color=#3366CC>Mississippi River</color>. The survey respondents as a whole showed just how little
agreement there was on the boundaries of the West.
Subregions
The region is split into two smaller units or divisions, by the U.S. Census Bureau:

<color=#3366CC>Mountain states</color>: <color=#3366CC>Montana</color>, <color=#3366CC>Wyoming</color>, <color=#3366CC>Colorado</color>, <color=#3366CC>New Mexico</color>, <color=#3366CC>Idaho</color>, <color=#3366CC>Utah</color>, <color=#3366CC>Arizona</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Nevada</color> Pacific states:
<color=#3366CC>Washington</color>, <color=#3366CC>Oregon</color>, <color=#3366CC>California</color>, <color=#3366CC>Alaska</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Hawaii</color>
Other classifications distinguish between <color=#3366CC>Southwest</color> and Northwest. Arizona, New Mexico, West Texas, and the
Oklahoma panhandle are typically considered to be the Southwest states. Meanwhile, the states of Montana, Idaho,
Oregon, and Washington can be considered part of the Northwest or <color=#3366CC>Pacific Northwest</color>.
The term West Coast is commonly used to refer to just California, Oregon, Washington, and Alaska, whereas Hawaii is
more geographically isolated from the continental U.S. and does not necessarily fit in any of these subregions.
Outlying areas

The three inhabited <color=#3366CC>Pacific</color> <color=#3366CC>U.S. territories</color> (<color=#3366CC>American Samoa</color>, <color=#3366CC>Guam</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Northern Mariana Islands</color>) are sometimes
considered part of the Western United States. American Samoa is in <color=#3366CC>Polynesia</color> in the <color=#3366CC>South Pacific Ocean</color>, while Guam
and the Northern Mariana Islands are in the <color=#3366CC>Mariana Islands</color> in the western <color=#3366CC>North Pacific Ocean</color>. Guam and the
Northern Mariana Islands have district courts within the 9th Circuit, which includes western states such as California
and Nevada. (See District Court of Guam and District Court for the Northern Mariana Islands). American Samoa,
Guam, and the Northern Mariana Islands are also considered part of the western U.S. by the U.S. National Park
Service, the Federal Reserve Bank system, FEMA, and the USGS.
Demographics
The population distribution by race in the Western United States (2022):
• 51.9% White (47.1% non-Hispanic)
• 30.8% Hispanic or Latino ethnicity (of any race)
• 10.8% Asian (10.6% non-Hispanic)
• 4.5% <color=#3366CC>Black</color> or <color=#3366CC>African-American</color> (4.3% non-Hispanic)
• 1.9% <color=#3366CC>American Indian</color> or Alaska Native (1.1% non-Hispanic)
• 0.6% Pacific Islander (0.6% non-Hispanic)
• 13.3% Some other race (0.6% non-Hispanic)
• 17.0% Two or more races (5.0% non-Hispanic)
As defined by the United States Census Bureau, the Western <color=#3366CC>region</color> of the United States includes 13 states, with a
total 2020 population of 78,588,572.
The West is one of the most sparsely settled areas in the United States with 49.5 /mi2. Only <color=#3366CC>Texas</color> with 78.0 /mi2,
<color=#3366CC>Washington</color> with 86.0 /mi2, and <color=#3366CC>California</color> with 213.4 /mi2 exceed the national average of 77.98 /mi2. As of 2022, just
under half of the 78.7 million residents of the West live in California.
The entire Western region has also been strongly influenced by European, Hispanic or Latino, Asian and <color=#3366CC>Native</color>
<color=#3366CC>Americans</color>; it contains the largest number of minorities in the U.S. While most of the studies of racial dynamics in
America such as riots in <color=#3366CC>Los Angeles</color> have been written about European and <color=#3366CC>African Americans</color>, in many cities in the
West and <color=#3366CC>California</color>, whites and blacks together are less than half the population because of the preference for the
region by Hispanics and Asians. African and European Americans, however, continue to wield a stronger political
influence because of the lower rates of citizenship and voting among Asians and Hispanics.
According to 2022 estimates from the Census Bureau, the largest ancestries reported in the West are Mexican
(24.2%), German (10.1%), English (9.5%), Irish (7.2%), Italian (3.5%), Filipino (3.4%), and Chinese (3.3%).
The West also contains much of the <color=#3366CC>Native American</color> population in the U.S., particularly in the large <color=#3366CC>reservations</color> in the

<color=#3366CC>Mountain</color> and <color=#3366CC>Desert States</color>. As of 2022, the West is home to 365,351 <color=#3366CC>Navajo</color>, 109,208 <color=#3366CC>Apache</color>, and 78,364 Blackfeet,
as well as 276,082 people identifying as <color=#3366CC>Indigenous Mexican</color>.

The largest concentrations for <color=#3366CC>African Americans</color> in the West can be found in <color=#3366CC>San Diego</color>, <color=#3366CC>Los Angeles</color>, <color=#3366CC>Oakland</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Sacramento</color>, <color=#3366CC>Fresno</color>, <color=#3366CC>San Francisco</color>, <color=#3366CC>Seattle</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tacoma</color>, <color=#3366CC>Phoenix</color>, <color=#3366CC>Las Vegas</color>, <color=#3366CC>Denver</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Colorado Springs</color>.
The Western United States has a higher sex ratio than any other region in the United States.
Because the tide of development had not yet reached most of the West when conservation became a national issue,
agencies of the <color=#3366CC>federal government</color> own and manage vast areas of land. (The most important among these are the
National Park Service and the Bureau of Land Management within the Interior Department, and the U.S. Forest Service
within the Agriculture Department.) <color=#3366CC>National parks</color> are reserved for recreational activities such as <color=#3366CC>fishing</color>, <color=#3366CC>camping</color>,

<color=#3366CC>hiking</color>, and boating, but other government lands also allow commercial activities like <color=#3366CC>ranching</color>, <color=#3366CC>logging</color>, and <color=#3366CC>mining</color>. In
recent years, some local residents who earn their livelihoods on federal land have come into conflict with the land's
managers, who are required to keep land use within environmentally acceptable limits.
The largest city in the region is <color=#3366CC>Los Angeles</color>, located on the West Coast. Other West Coast cities include <color=#3366CC>San Diego</color>,

San Bernardino, <color=#3366CC>San Jose</color>, <color=#3366CC>San Francisco</color>, <color=#3366CC>Oakland</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bakersfield</color>, <color=#3366CC>Fresno</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sacramento</color>, <color=#3366CC>Seattle</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tacoma</color>, <color=#3366CC>Anchorage</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Spokane</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Portland</color> – some of which are dozens of miles inland. Prominent cities in the <color=#3366CC>Mountain States</color> include

<color=#3366CC>Denver</color>, <color=#3366CC>Colorado Springs</color>, <color=#3366CC>Phoenix</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tucson</color>, <color=#3366CC>Albuquerque</color>, <color=#3366CC>Las Vegas</color>, <color=#3366CC>Reno</color>, <color=#3366CC>Salt Lake City</color>, <color=#3366CC>Boise</color>, <color=#3366CC>Billings</color>, and
Missoula.
Natural geography
Along the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Ocean</color> coast lie the <color=#3366CC>Coast Ranges</color>, which, while not approaching the scale of the <color=#3366CC>Rocky Mountains</color>,
are formidable nevertheless. They collect a large part of the airborne moisture moving in from the ocean. East of the
Coast Ranges lie several cultivated fertile <color=#3366CC>valleys</color>, notably the San Joaquin and Sacramento valleys of <color=#3366CC>California</color> and
the <color=#3366CC>Willamette Valley</color> of <color=#3366CC>Oregon</color>.
Beyond the valleys lie the <color=#3366CC>Sierra Nevada</color> in the south and the <color=#3366CC>Cascade Range</color> in the north. <color=#3366CC>Mount Whitney</color>, at 14505 ft
the tallest peak in the contiguous 48 states, is in the Sierra Nevada. The Cascades are also volcanic. <color=#3366CC>Mount Rainier</color>, a
volcano in <color=#3366CC>Washington</color>, is also over 14000 ft. <color=#3366CC>Mount St. Helens</color>, a volcano in the Cascades, erupted explosively in
1980. A major volcanic eruption at Mount Mazama around 4860 BC formed <color=#3366CC>Crater Lake</color>. These mountain ranges see
heavy precipitation, capturing most of the moisture that remains after the Coast Ranges, and creating a <color=#3366CC>rain shadow</color> to
the east forming vast stretches of arid land. These dry areas encompass much of <color=#3366CC>Nevada</color>, <color=#3366CC>Utah</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Arizona</color>. The
<color=#3366CC>Mojave Desert</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sonoran Desert</color> along with other deserts are found here.
Beyond the deserts lie the <color=#3366CC>Rocky Mountains</color>. In the north, they run almost immediately east of the <color=#3366CC>Cascade Range</color>, so
that the desert region is only a few miles wide by the time one reaches the Canada–US border. The Rockies are
hundreds of miles wide and run uninterrupted from <color=#3366CC>New Mexico</color> to <color=#3366CC>Alaska</color>. The Rocky Mountain Region is the highest
overall area of the United States, with an average elevation of above 4000 ft. The tallest peaks of the Rockies, 54 of
which are over 14000 ft, are found in central and western <color=#3366CC>Colorado</color>. East of the Rocky Mountains is the Great Plains,
the western portions (for example, the eastern half of Colorado) of which are generally considered to be part of the
western United States.
The West has several long rivers that empty into the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Ocean</color>, while the eastern rivers run into the <color=#3366CC>Gulf of Mexico</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>Mississippi River</color> forms the easternmost possible boundary for the West today. The <color=#3366CC>Missouri River</color>, a tributary of
the Mississippi, flows from its headwaters in the <color=#3366CC>Rocky Mountains</color> eastward across the <color=#3366CC>Great Plains</color>, a vast <color=#3366CC>grassy</color>
plateau, before sloping gradually down to the forests and hence to the Mississippi. The <color=#3366CC>Colorado River</color> snakes through
the <color=#3366CC>Mountain states</color>, at one point forming the <color=#3366CC>Grand Canyon</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>Colorado River</color> is a major source of water in the Southwest and many dams, such as the <color=#3366CC>Hoover Dam</color>, form
reservoirs along it. So much water is drawn for drinking water throughout the West and irrigation in <color=#3366CC>California</color> that in
most years, water from the Colorado River no longer reaches the <color=#3366CC>Gulf of California</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Columbia River</color>, the largest
river in volume flowing into the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Ocean</color> from <color=#3366CC>North America</color>, and its tributary, the <color=#3366CC>Snake River</color>, water the Pacific
Northwest. The <color=#3366CC>Platte</color> runs through <color=#3366CC>Nebraska</color> and was known for being a mile (2 km) wide but only a half-inch (1 cm)

deep. The <color=#3366CC>Rio Grande</color> forms the border between <color=#3366CC>Texas</color> and <color=#3366CC>Mexico</color> before turning due north and splitting <color=#3366CC>New Mexico</color>
in half.
According to the United States Coast Guard, "The Western Rivers System consists of the <color=#3366CC>Mississippi</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ohio</color>, <color=#3366CC>Missouri</color>,

Illinois, <color=#3366CC>Tennessee</color>, <color=#3366CC>Cumberland</color>, <color=#3366CC>Arkansas</color>, and <color=#3366CC>White Rivers</color> and their tributaries, and certain other rivers that flow
towards the <color=#3366CC>Gulf of Mexico</color>." The Ohio River portion of the system includes parts of several Atlantic coastal states, from
Georgia to New York.
Climate and agriculture
Most of the public land held by the U.S. National Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management is in the Western
states. Public lands account for 25 to 75 percent of the total land area in these states.
The climate of the West is <color=#3366CC>semi-arid</color>, yet parts of the region get high amounts of rain or snow. Other parts are true
desert which receive less than 5 in of rain per year. The climate is increasingly unstable, and subject to periods of
severe drought.
The seasonal temperatures vary greatly throughout the West. Low elevations on the West Coast have warm summers
and mild winters with little to no snow. The <color=#3366CC>desert southwest</color> has very hot summers and mild winters. While the
mountains in the southwest receive generally large amounts of snow. The Inland Northwest has a <color=#3366CC>continental climate</color> of
warm to hot summers and cold to bitterly cold winters.
Annual rainfall is greater in the eastern portions, gradually tapering off until reaching the Pacific Coast where it
increases again. In fact, the greatest annual rainfall in the United States falls in the coastal regions of the <color=#3366CC>Pacific</color>
<color=#3366CC>Northwest</color>. Drought is much more common in the West than the rest of the United States. The driest place recorded in
the United States is <color=#3366CC>Death Valley</color>, California. In Western states, drought is closely associated with fire risk, and there
have been a number of notable wildfires causing extensive property damage and wildlife <color=#3366CC>habitat destruction</color>. The
Western United States is predicted to experience drought-like conditions for much of the 21st century.
Violent thunderstorms occur east of the <color=#3366CC>Rockies</color>. <color=#3366CC>Tornadoes</color> occur every spring on the southern plains, with the most
common and most destructive centered on Tornado Alley, which covers eastern portions of the West, (<color=#3366CC>Texas</color> to <color=#3366CC>North</color>
<color=#3366CC>Dakota</color>), and all states in between and to the east.
Agriculture varies depending on rainfall, irrigation, soil, elevation, and temperature extremes. The arid regions generally
support only livestock grazing, chiefly beef cattle. The wheat belt extends from <color=#3366CC>Texas</color> through The Dakotas, producing
most of the wheat and soybeans in the U.S. and exporting more to the rest of the world. Irrigation in the <color=#3366CC>Southwest</color>
allows the growth of great quantities of fruits, nuts, and vegetables as well as grain, hay, and flowers. Texas is a major
cattle and sheep raising area, as well as the nation's largest producer of cotton. <color=#3366CC>Washington</color> is famous for its apples,

and <color=#3366CC>Idaho</color> for its potatoes. <color=#3366CC>California</color> and <color=#3366CC>Arizona</color> are major producers of <color=#3366CC>citrus</color> crops, however, declining supplies of
water, as well as urban sprawl have contributed to a sharp decline in citrus production in Arizona. Many varieties of
chile peppers are grown in the valleys of <color=#3366CC>New Mexico</color>.
Starting in 1902, Congress passed a series of acts authorizing the establishment of the United States Bureau of
Reclamation to oversee water development projects in seventeen western states.
During the first half of the 20th century, dams and irrigation projects provided water for rapid agricultural growth
throughout the West and brought prosperity for several states, where agriculture had previously only been subsistence
level. Following <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>, the West's cities experienced an economic and population boom. The population growth,

mostly in the <color=#3366CC>Southwest</color> states of <color=#3366CC>New Mexico</color>, <color=#3366CC>Utah</color>, <color=#3366CC>Colorado</color>, <color=#3366CC>Arizona</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Nevada</color>, has strained water and power
resources, with water diverted from agricultural uses to major population centers, such as the Las Vegas Valley and
<color=#3366CC>Los Angeles</color>.
Geology
Plains make up much of the eastern portion of the West, underlain with sedimentary rock from the Upper <color=#3366CC>Paleozoic</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Mesozoic</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Cenozoic</color> eras. The <color=#3366CC>Rocky Mountains</color> expose igneous and metamorphic rock both from the
<color=#3366CC>Precambrian</color> and from the <color=#3366CC>Phanerozoic</color> eon. The Intermountain States and <color=#3366CC>Pacific Northwest</color> have huge expanses of
volcanic rock from the Cenozoic era. <color=#3366CC>Salt flats</color> and salt lakes reveal a time when the great inland seas covered much of
what is now the West.
The Pacific states are the most geologically active areas in the United States. <color=#3366CC>Earthquakes</color> cause damage every few to
several years in <color=#3366CC>California</color>. While the Pacific states are the most volcanically active areas, extinct <color=#3366CC>volcanoes</color> and lava
flows are found throughout most of the West.
Wildlife
History
The Western United States has been populated by <color=#3366CC>Native Americans</color> since at least 11,000 years ago, when the first
Paleo-Indians arrived. Pre-Columbian trade routes to kingdoms and empires such as the Mound Builders existed in
places such as <color=#3366CC>Yellowstone National Park</color> since around 1000 AD. Major settlement of the western territories developed
rapidly in the 1840s, largely through the <color=#3366CC>Oregon Trail</color> and the <color=#3366CC>California Gold Rush</color> of 1849. <color=#3366CC>California</color> experienced
such a rapid growth in a few short months that it was admitted to statehood in 1850 without the normal transitory phase
of becoming an official territory.
One of the largest migrations in American history occurred in the 1840s as the Latter Day Saints left the <color=#3366CC>Midwest</color> to
build a theocracy in <color=#3366CC>Utah</color>.
Both <color=#3366CC>Omaha, Nebraska</color> and <color=#3366CC>St. Louis, Missouri</color> laid claim to the title, "Gateway to the West" during this period. Omaha,
home to the <color=#3366CC>Union Pacific Railroad</color> and the Mormon Trail, made its fortunes on outfitting settlers; St. Louis built itself
upon the vast <color=#3366CC>fur trade</color> in the West before its settlement.
The 1850s were marked by political battles over the expansion of slavery into the western territories, issues leading to
the Civil War.
Between 1863 and 1869, North America's first transcontinental railroad was constructed to connect the eastern US with
the Pacific coast. The resulting railroad connection revolutionized the settlement and economy of the American West by
making the transportation of passengers and freight quicker, safer, and cheaper.
The history of the American West in the late 19th and early 20th centuries has acquired a cultural mythos in the
literature and cinema of the United States. The image of the <color=#3366CC>cowboy</color>, the homesteader, and <color=#3366CC>westward expansion</color> took
real events and transmuted them into a myth of the west which has shaped much of American popular culture since the
late 19th century.
Writers as diverse as <color=#3366CC>Bret Harte</color> and <color=#3366CC>Zane Grey</color> celebrated or derided cowboy culture, while artists such as <color=#3366CC>Frederic</color>
<color=#3366CC>Remington</color> created Western art as a method of recording the expansion into the west. The <color=#3366CC>American cinema</color>, in
particular, created the genre of the <color=#3366CC>Western movie</color>, which, in many cases, use the West as a metaphor for the virtue of
self-reliance and an American ethos. The contrast between the romanticism of culture about the West and the actuality
of the history of the westward expansion has been a theme of late 20th and early 21st century scholarship about the
West. Cowboy culture has become embedded in the American experience as a common cultural touchstone, and
modern forms as diverse as <color=#3366CC>country and western music</color> have celebrated the sense of isolation and independence of
spirit inspired by the frontiersmen on "virgin land".
20th century
The advent of the <color=#3366CC>automobile</color> enabled the average American to tour the West. Western businessmen promoted <color=#3366CC>Route</color>
<color=#3366CC>66</color> as a means to bring tourism and industry to the West. In the 1950s, representatives from all the western states built
the Cowboy Hall of Fame and Western Heritage Center to showcase western culture and greet travelers from the East.
During the latter half of the 20th century, several transcontinental interstate highways crossed the West bringing more
trade and tourists from the East. Oil boom towns in <color=#3366CC>Texas</color> and <color=#3366CC>Oklahoma</color> rivaled the old mining camps for their
rawness and wealth. The <color=#3366CC>Dust Bowl</color> forced children of the original homesteaders even further west.
The movies became America's chief entertainment source featuring <color=#3366CC>western fiction</color>, later the community of <color=#3366CC>Hollywood</color>
in <color=#3366CC>Los Angeles</color> became the headquarters of the <color=#3366CC>mass media</color> such as radio and television production.
California has emerged as the most populous state and one of the top 10 economies in the world. Massive late
19th–20th century population and settlement booms created two <color=#3366CC>megalopolis</color> areas of the Greater Los
Angeles/<color=#3366CC>Southern California</color> and the <color=#3366CC>San Francisco Bay Area</color>/<color=#3366CC>Northern California</color> regions, one of the nation's largest
metropolitan areas and in the top 25 largest urban areas in the world. Five more metropolitan areas of San

Bernardino-Riverside, <color=#3366CC>San Diego</color>, <color=#3366CC>Denver</color>, <color=#3366CC>Phoenix</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Seattle</color> have over a million residents, while the three fastest
growing metro areas were the Salt Lake City metropolitan area, the Las Vegas metropolitan area; and the Portland
metropolitan area.
Since the mid-1970s, historians of the West have emphasized the <color=#3366CC>World War II</color> years as a major watershed, as a
region experienced enormous social and economic change, and became the pacesetter for <color=#3366CC>societal evolution</color>. The
population soared, especially in metropolitan areas, as a result of massive expansion of the manufacture of airplanes,
ships and munitions and of military and Naval training facilities. California upgraded universities to world-class status,
intensified scientific research, and expanded infrastructure. After the war millions more migrated using the GI Bill to buy
suburban homes, many of them recalling rewarding wartime experience in military training facilities. The region had
always been more democratic with greater racial and <color=#3366CC>gender equality</color>, and continued as a national pacesetter in
modernization. New problems emerged, especially environmental issues where westerners took the lead in areas such
as the allocation of scarce water resources as well as dealing with smog and air pollution. More recently historians
have looked at nuances, pointing out that some of the trends began before 1941.
<color=#3366CC>Los Angeles</color> has the largest Mexican population outside of <color=#3366CC>Mexico</color>, while <color=#3366CC>San Francisco</color> has the largest Chinese
community in <color=#3366CC>North America</color> and also has a large <color=#3366CC>LGBT</color> community, and <color=#3366CC>Oakland, California</color> has a large percentage of
residents being <color=#3366CC>African-American</color>, as well as <color=#3366CC>Long Beach, California</color> which also has a significant black community. The
state of <color=#3366CC>Utah</color> has a Mormon majority (estimated at 62.4% in 2004), while some cities like <color=#3366CC>Albuquerque, New Mexico</color>;

<color=#3366CC>Billings, Montana</color>; <color=#3366CC>Spokane, Washington</color>; and <color=#3366CC>Tucson, Arizona</color> are located near <color=#3366CC>Indian reservations</color>. In remote areas
there are settlements of Alaskan Natives and <color=#3366CC>Native Hawaiians</color>.
Culture
Historically, the traditional culture of the Western United States has been defined by the cowboys, pioneers, and <color=#3366CC>Native</color>

<color=#3366CC>Americans</color> who first inhabited the <color=#3366CC>Wild West</color>. The sparse geography of the western deserts (<color=#3366CC>Mojave Desert</color>, <color=#3366CC>Great</color>
<color=#3366CC>Basin Desert</color>) and isolated small <color=#3366CC>towns</color>, combined with the broad freeways (<color=#3366CC>U.S. Route 66</color>) and long railroads (First
transcontinental railroad), have contributed to the popular image of the west as a desolate, open space full of unending
roads.
Facing both the Pacific Ocean and the <color=#3366CC>Mexican</color> border, the West has been shaped by a variety of ethnic groups.
<color=#3366CC>Hawaii</color> is the only state in the union in which Asian Americans outnumber white American residents. People from many
countries in Asia settled in <color=#3366CC>California</color> and other coastal states in several waves of immigration since the 19th century,
contributing to the <color=#3366CC>Gold rush</color>, the building of the transcontinental railroad, agriculture, and more recently, high
technology.

The border states—<color=#3366CC>California</color>, <color=#3366CC>Arizona</color>, <color=#3366CC>New Mexico</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Texas</color>—and other southwestern states such as <color=#3366CC>Colorado</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Utah</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Nevada</color> all have large Hispanic populations, and the many <color=#3366CC>Spanish</color> place names attest to their history as
former Spanish and Mexican territories. Mexican-Americans have also had a growing population in Northwestern states
of <color=#3366CC>Oregon</color> and <color=#3366CC>Washington</color>, as well as the southern states of Texas and <color=#3366CC>Oklahoma</color>.
In the Pacific States, the wide areas filled with small towns, farms, and forests are supplemented by a few big port cities
which have evolved into world centers for the media and technology industries. Now the second largest city in the
nation, <color=#3366CC>Los Angeles</color> is best known as the home of the <color=#3366CC>Hollywood</color> <color=#3366CC>film</color> industry; the area around Los Angeles also was a
major center for the aerospace industry by <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>, though Boeing, located in <color=#3366CC>Washington state</color> would lead the
aerospace industry. Fueled by the growth of Los Angeles, as well as the <color=#3366CC>San Francisco Bay area</color>, including <color=#3366CC>Silicon</color>
<color=#3366CC>Valley</color>, the center of America's high tech industry, <color=#3366CC>California</color> has become the most populous of all the 50 states. <color=#3366CC>Oregon</color>
and Washington have also seen rapid growth with the rise of <color=#3366CC>Boeing</color> and <color=#3366CC>Microsoft</color> along with agriculture and resource
based industries.
<color=#3366CC>Alaska</color>—the northernmost state in the Union—is a vast land of few people, many of them native, and of great stretches
of wilderness, protected in <color=#3366CC>national parks</color> and <color=#3366CC>wildlife refuges</color>. Hawaii's location makes it a major gateway between the
United States and Asia, as well as a center for tourism.

The <color=#3366CC>Mountain States</color> subregion includes <color=#3366CC>Arizona</color>, <color=#3366CC>Colorado</color>, <color=#3366CC>Idaho</color>, <color=#3366CC>Montana</color>, <color=#3366CC>Nevada</color>, <color=#3366CC>New Mexico</color>, <color=#3366CC>Utah</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>Wyoming</color>. The mountain states have relatively low population densities, and developed as ranching and mining areas
that only recently became urbanized. Most of them have highly individualistic cultures, and have worked to balance the
interests of urban development, recreation, and the environment.
Culturally distinctive points of the mountain states include the large Mormon population in the Mormon Corridor,

including southeastern <color=#3366CC>Idaho</color>, <color=#3366CC>Utah</color>, Northern <color=#3366CC>Arizona</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Nevada</color>; the extravagant <color=#3366CC>casino</color> resort towns of Las Vegas
and <color=#3366CC>Reno</color>, Nevada; and the numerous <color=#3366CC>American Indian</color> tribal reservations.

Politics
The region's distance from historical centers of power in the East, and the celebrated "frontier spirit" of its settlers offer
two clichés for explaining the region's independent, heterogeneous politics. Historically, the West was the first region to
see widespread women's suffrage, with women casting votes in <color=#3366CC>Utah</color> and <color=#3366CC>Wyoming</color> as early as 1870, five decades
before the 19th Amendment was ratified by the nation. <color=#3366CC>California</color> birthed both the <color=#3366CC>property rights</color> and conservation
movements, and spawned such phenomena as the Taxpayer Revolt and the Berkeley Free Speech Movement. It has
also produced three presidents: <color=#3366CC>Herbert Hoover</color>, <color=#3366CC>Richard Nixon</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Ronald Reagan</color>.
The prevalence of <color=#3366CC>libertarian</color> political attitudes is widespread. For example, the majority of Western states have

legalized <color=#3366CC>medicinal marijuana</color> (all but <color=#3366CC>Idaho</color> and <color=#3366CC>Wyoming</color>) and some forms of gambling (except <color=#3366CC>Utah</color>); <color=#3366CC>Colorado</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Oregon</color>, <color=#3366CC>Washington</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Montana</color> have legalized physician-assisted suicide; most rural counties in <color=#3366CC>Nevada</color> allow
licensed brothels, and voters in <color=#3366CC>Alaska</color>, Colorado, Nevada, <color=#3366CC>California</color>, Oregon, and Washington have legalized
recreational use of marijuana.

<color=#3366CC>California</color>, <color=#3366CC>Oregon</color>, <color=#3366CC>Washington</color>, <color=#3366CC>Nevada</color>, <color=#3366CC>Colorado</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hawaii</color> and <color=#3366CC>New Mexico</color> lean toward the <color=#3366CC>Democratic Party</color>. In
recent times, as seen in the 2020 United States presidential election and 2022 Arizona gubernatorial election, <color=#3366CC>Arizona</color>
is also beginning to lean towards the Democratic Party as well. <color=#3366CC>San Francisco</color>'s two main political parties are the Green
Party and the Democratic Party. One of the longest-serving Democratic congressional leaders is from the region:
former Speaker of the United States House of Representatives <color=#3366CC>Nancy Pelosi</color> of California.

<color=#3366CC>Alaska</color> and most <color=#3366CC>Mountain states</color> are more <color=#3366CC>Republican</color>, with Alaska, <color=#3366CC>Idaho</color>, <color=#3366CC>Montana</color>, <color=#3366CC>Utah</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Wyoming</color> being
Republican strongholds. The state of <color=#3366CC>Arizona</color> has been won by the Republican presidential candidate in every election
except three times since 1948, but in 2020 Arizona voted Democratic. Also, in 2018 and 2020, the GOP lost both U.S.
Senate seats in Arizona to the Democrats. The states of Idaho, Utah, and Wyoming have been won by every
Republican presidential nominee since 1964.
The state of <color=#3366CC>Nevada</color> is considered a political bellwether, having correctly voted for every president except twice (in
1976 and 2016) since 1912. <color=#3366CC>New Mexico</color> too is considered a bellwether, having voted for the popular vote winner in
every presidential election since statehood, except in 1976 and 2024.
As the fastest-growing demographic group, after <color=#3366CC>Asians</color>, Latinos are hotly contested by both parties. Immigration is an
important political issue for this group. Backlash against undocumented immigrants led to the passage of California
Proposition 187 in 1994, a ballot initiative which would have denied many public services to them. Association of this
proposal with California Republicans, especially incumbent governor Pete Wilson, drove many Hispanic voters to the
Democrats.

Health
The Western United States consistently ranks well in health measures. The rate of potentially preventable
hospitalizations in the Western United States was consistently lower than other regions from 2005 to 2011. While the
proportion of maternal or neonatal hospital stays was higher in the Western United States relative to other regions, the
proportion of medical stays in hospitals was lower than in other regions in 2012.
Brenda Fricker
Brenda Fricker (17 February 1945 – 16 July 2026) was an Irish actress whose career spanned six decades on stage
and screen. She appeared in more than 30 films and television productions. In 1990, Fricker became the first Irish
actress to win an <color=#3366CC>Academy Award</color>, earning the award for Best Supporting Actress for the biopic My Left Foot (1989).
She also appeared in films such as The Field (1990), Home Alone 2: Lost in New York (1992), So I Married an Axe
Murderer (1993), Angels in the Outfield (1994), A Time to Kill (1996), Veronica Guerin (2003), Inside I'm Dancing
(2004), and Albert Nobbs (2011).
Fricker was honoured with the inaugural <color=#3366CC>Maureen O'Hara</color> Award at the Kerry Film Festival in 2008. In 2020, The Irish
Times ranked her 26th on its list of the greatest Irish film actors of all time.
Early life
Brenda Fricker was born on 17 February 1945 in <color=#3366CC>Dublin</color>, Ireland. Her mother "Bina" (née Murphy) was from
Gneeveguilla, County Kerry. Bina taught languages at Stratford College in Rathgar, and Fricker's father, Desmond
Frederick Fricker, worked in the Department of Agriculture, and as "Fred Desmond", was a broadcaster with RTÉ and a
journalist for The Irish Times.
Before becoming an actress, Fricker was an assistant to the art editor of The Irish Times, with hopes of becoming a
reporter. She became an actress "by chance". Fricker's feature-film career began with a small, uncredited part in the
1964 film Of Human Bondage, based on <color=#3366CC>W. Somerset Maugham's 1915 novel</color>. She also appeared in Tolka Row,
Ireland's first soap opera.
Career
One of Fricker's first television roles was staff nurse Maloney in <color=#3366CC>Coronation Street</color>. She came to wider public attention
in the United Kingdom in another nursing role, as Megan Roach in the BBC One drama series Casualty.
Fricker achieved international acclaim after winning the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress in 1990 for her
performance as Christy Brown's mother in My Left Foot (1989). In her acceptance speech, Fricker thanked Brown "just
for being alive" and dedicated the Oscar to Brown's mother, saying that "anybody who gives birth 22 times deserves
one of these". For her performance, Fricker was also nominated for a <color=#3366CC>Golden Globe</color>, and she won the Los Angeles Film
Critics Association Award for Best Supporting Actress. She rejoined My Left Foot writer and director Jim Sheridan for
The Field (1990), starring alongside <color=#3366CC>Richard Harris</color> as Maggie McCabe, the wife of Harris's "Bull" McCabe. Fricker
continued her television work during this period, appearing in the Australian-produced short series Brides of Christ
(1991) and the miniseries Seekers (1992), produced by Sarah Lawson and co-starring Josette Simon.
Buoyed by her Oscar win, Fricker went on to appear in several high-profile Hollywood films, most notably Home Alone
2: Lost in New York (1992) as the <color=#3366CC>Central Park</color> Pigeon Lady. In 1993, she portrayed May Mackenzie, the Weekly World
News-obsessed Scottish mother of <color=#3366CC>Mike Myers</color>'s Charlie Mackenzie, in So I Married an Axe Murderer. The following
year, Fricker played Maggie, the motherly caretaker of Joseph Gordon-Levitt's character, in the family comedy Angels
in the Outfield. One of her final Hollywood roles was Ethel Twitty in A Time to Kill (1996), after which Fricker focused
mainly on film and television work in Canada, Ireland, and the United Kingdom. In 2003, she played Bernie Guerin,
mother of <color=#3366CC>Veronica Guerin</color> (portrayed by <color=#3366CC>Cate Blanchett</color>) in the film of the same name. Fricker then appeared as nurse
Eileen in Inside I'm Dancing (2004). Her other notable roles include Nuala O'Loan in Omagh (2004), Gráinne
McFadden in the docudrama No Tears about women infected with <color=#3366CC>hepatitis C</color> through the Anti-D blood product in the
1970s, Aunt Maeve in Durango (1999), and Heather Nightingale in How About You (2007), based on a short story by
Maeve Binchy.
Fricker appeared in Closing the Ring, <color=#3366CC>Richard Attenborough</color>'s post-<color=#3366CC>World War II</color> drama, also starring <color=#3366CC>Shirley MacLaine</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Christopher Plummer</color>, and Mischa Barton. She played half of a lesbian couple alongside <color=#3366CC>Olympia Dukakis</color> in
Cloudburst (2011). In 2012, Fricker's supporting role in Albert Nobbs earned her an Irish Film and Television Award
nomination.
In 2021, Fricker joined the cast of the TV adaptation of Holding, based on the novel by <color=#3366CC>Graham Norton</color>, marking her
first major onscreen role in six years. Three years later, Fricker starred in experimental documentarian Tadhg
O'Sullivan's first fiction drama, The Swallow, giving a solitary performance as an unnamed elderly woman reflecting on
her life.
Personal life and death
Fricker was married to Barry Davis from 1979 until they separated nine years later. She was pregnant six times during
the marriage, but each pregnancy ended in miscarriage. Davis, who struggled with alcoholism, died in 1990. On The
Tommy Tiernan Show in 2021, Fricker said that she had battled severe depression for much of her life, including being
hospitalised many times.
Fricker said that her loves included her pet dogs, drinking <color=#3366CC>Guinness</color>, reading poetry, and playing <color=#3366CC>snooker</color> – she once
remarked that she had taken on the entire crew of My Left Foot: "I played pool against 17 of them, and beat them all!"
In 2012, Fricker said "Of all the films I've made, only three do I remember where I felt I'd moved forward as an actress:
Cloudburst, My Left Foot, and The Field."
In her 2025 memoir She Died Young: A Life in Fragments, Fricker wrote that she was physically abused by her mother
and sexually abused by a teacher when she was eight. At age 14, Fricker spent two years in hospital after going
through a car windscreen in a cycling accident, later developed <color=#3366CC>tuberculosis</color>, and made repeated suicide attempts that
led to periods in psychiatric care. She said that she was raped at age 17 and described another assault early in her
career. Fricker also wrote that she began <color=#3366CC>self-harming</color> before age 10, influenced by religious imagery she saw in
church.
Fricker died in Dublin on 16 July 2026, aged 81, after a period of ill health. Her funeral took place on 6 August at St
Catherine's Church on Meath Street, followed by a private burial. Attendees included actor Brendan Gleeson, musician
Frankie Gavin, and broadcaster Ray D'Arcy.
Awards and recognition
In 2020, The Irish Times ranked Fricker 26th on its list of the 50 greatest Irish film actors of all time.

Quinine
Quinine is a medication used to treat <color=#3366CC>malaria</color> and babesiosis. This includes the treatment of malaria due to Plasmodium
falciparum that is resistant to <color=#3366CC>chloroquine</color> when artesunate is not available. While sometimes used for <color=#3366CC>nocturnal leg</color>
<color=#3366CC>cramps</color>, quinine is not recommended for this purpose due to the risk of serious <color=#3366CC>side effects</color>. It can be taken by mouth or
<color=#3366CC>intravenously</color>. Malaria resistance to quinine occurs in certain areas of the world. Quinine is also used as an ingredient
in <color=#3366CC>tonic water</color> and other beverages to impart a bitter taste.
Common side effects include headache, <color=#3366CC>ringing in the ears</color>, vision issues, and <color=#3366CC>sweating</color>. More severe side effects
include <color=#3366CC>deafness</color>, low blood platelets, and an <color=#3366CC>irregular heartbeat</color>. Use can make one more prone to <color=#3366CC>sunburn</color>. While it is
unclear if use during pregnancy carries potential for fetal harm, treating malaria during pregnancy with quinine when
appropriate is still recommended. Quinine is an <color=#3366CC>alkaloid</color>, a naturally occurring chemical compound. It possesses a
C9H7N quinoline <color=#3366CC>functional group</color> (<color=#3366CC>pyridine</color> fused to <color=#3366CC>benzene</color>).
Quinine was first isolated in 1820 from the bark of a cinchona tree, which is native to <color=#3366CC>Peru</color>, and its molecular formula
was determined by Adolph Strecker in 1854. The class of chemical compounds to which it belongs is thus called the
cinchona alkaloids. Bark extracts had been used to treat malaria since at least 1632 and it was introduced to Spain as
early as 1636 by <color=#3366CC>Jesuit missionaries</color> returning from the <color=#3366CC>New World</color>. It is on the <color=#3366CC>World Health Organization's List of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Essential Medicines</color>. Treatment of malaria with quinine marks the first known use of a chemical compound to treat an
infectious disease.
Uses
Medical
As of 2006, quinine is no longer recommended by the <color=#3366CC>World Health Organization</color> (WHO) as a first-line treatment for
<color=#3366CC>malaria</color>, because there are other substances that are equally effective with fewer side effects. They recommend that it
be used only when <color=#3366CC>artemisinins</color> are not available. Quinine is also used to treat <color=#3366CC>lupus</color> and <color=#3366CC>arthritis</color>.
Quinine was frequently prescribed as an off-label treatment for <color=#3366CC>leg cramps at night</color>, but this has become less common
since 2010 due to a warning from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) that such practice is associated with
life-threatening side effects. Quinine can also act as a competitive inhibitor of monoamine oxidase (MAO), an enzyme
that removes neurotransmitters from the brain. As an MAO inhibitor, it has potential to serve as a treatment for
individuals with psychological disorders, similar to antidepressants that inhibit MAO.
Available forms
Quinine is a basic <color=#3366CC>amine</color> and is usually provided as a salt. Various existing preparations include the hydrochloride,
dihydrochloride, <color=#3366CC>sulfate</color>, bisulfate and gluconate. In the United States, quinine sulfate is commercially available in 324
mg tablets under the brand name Qualaquin.
All quinine salts may be given orally or <color=#3366CC>intravenously</color> (IV); quinine gluconate may also be given intramuscularly (IM) or
rectally (PR). The main problem with rectal administration is that the dose can be expelled before it is completely
absorbed; in practice, this is corrected by giving a further half dose. No injectable preparation of quinine is licensed in
the US; quinidine is used instead.
Beverages
Quinine is a flavor component of <color=#3366CC>tonic water</color> and bitter lemon <color=#3366CC>soft drinks</color>. On the soda gun behind many bars, tonic
water is designated by the letter "Q" representing quinine.
Tonic water was initially marketed as a means of delivering quinine to consumers in order to offer anti-malarial
protection. According to tradition, because of the bitter taste of anti-<color=#3366CC>malarial</color> quinine tonic, British colonials in India
mixed it with <color=#3366CC>gin</color> to make it more palatable, thus creating the <color=#3366CC>gin and tonic</color> cocktail, which is still popular today. While it
is possible to drink enough tonic water to temporarily achieve quinine levels that offer anti-malarial protection, it is not a
sustainable long-term means of protection.
In France, quinine is an ingredient of an apéritif known as quinquina, or "Cap Corse", and the wine-based apéritif
Dubonnet. In Spain, quinine (also known as "Peruvian bark" for its origin from the native cinchona tree) is sometimes
blended into sweet Malaga wine, which is then called "Malaga Quina". In Italy, the traditional flavoured wine Barolo
Chinato is infused with quinine and local herbs, and is served as a digestif. In Britain, the company A.G. Barr uses
quinine as an ingredient in the carbonated and caffeinated beverage Irn-Bru. In Uruguay and Argentina, quinine is an
ingredient of a <color=#3366CC>PepsiCo</color> tonic water named Paso de los Toros. In Denmark, it is used as an ingredient in the carbonated
sports drink Faxe Kondi made by Royal Unibrew.
As a flavouring agent in drinks, quinine is limited to 83 <color=#3366CC>ppm</color> (83 mg/L) in the United States, to 85 mg/L in Taiwan, and to
100 mg/L in the European Union.
Direct use of cinchona bark in beverages is also allowed in the US, with a maximum allowed total cinchona alkaloid
level of 83 ppm in the finished beverage.
Scientific
Quinine (and quinidine) are used as the <color=#3366CC>chiral</color> moiety for the <color=#3366CC>ligands</color> used in Sharpless asymmetric dihydroxylation as
well as for numerous other chiral catalyst backbones. Because of its relatively constant and well-known <color=#3366CC>fluorescence</color>
quantum yield, quinine is used in <color=#3366CC>photochemistry</color> as a common fluorescence standard.
Contraindications
Because of the narrow difference between its therapeutic and toxic effects, quinine is a common cause of drug-induced
disorders, including thrombocytopenia and thrombotic microangiopathy. Even from minor levels occurring in common
beverages, quinine can have severe adverse effects involving multiple organ systems, among which are <color=#3366CC>immune</color>
<color=#3366CC>system</color> effects and <color=#3366CC>fever</color>, <color=#3366CC>hypotension</color>, hemolytic anemia, acute kidney injury, liver toxicity, and blindness. In people
with <color=#3366CC>atrial fibrillation</color>, conduction defects, or heart block, quinine can cause <color=#3366CC>heart arrhythmias</color>, and should be avoided.
Quinine can cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency (an inherited deficiency), but this risk is small and the physician
should not hesitate to use quinine in people with G6PD deficiency when there is no alternative.
While not necessarily an absolute contraindication, concomitant administration of quinine with drugs primarily
metabolized by CYP2D6 may lead to higher than expected plasma concentrations of the drug, due to quinine's strong
inhibition of the enzyme.
Adverse effects
Quinine can cause unpredictable serious and life-threatening blood and cardiovascular reactions including low platelet
count and hemolytic–uremic syndrome/thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (HUS/TTP), long QT syndrome and other
